newsitem.title: USA: Saudi dissident linked to bombing pleads innocent.
newsitem.headline: Saudi dissident linked to bombing pleads innocent.

text.p: A Saudi dissident on Wednesday pulled out of a plea deal to admit plotting an anti-American attack in the Middle East and in return help a U.S. investigation into a deadly truck bombing in Saudi Arabia.

The suspect, Hani al-Sayegh, who has been linked to the massive truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. servicemen in 1996, instead pleaded innocent to the charges of plotting an earlier attack against Americans that never was carried out.

His repudiation of the deal represented a major embarrassment for the U.S. government, which arranged Sayegh's deportation from Canada last month and hoped he might provide valuable information about those responsible for the bombing.
Asked by the judge how he would plead to the charges that carry a maximum penalty of life in prison, Sayegh responded in a clear voice, "Not guilty." That was his only comment.
His lawyer, Francis Carter, said at the hearing the still- secret plea agreement was invalid to begin with. He rejected claims by U.S. prosecutor Eric Dubelier that Sayegh had broken the deal.
"It's a dead letter," Carter said of the plea agreement that called for Sayegh to get up to 10 years in prison in return for his cooperation. "It no longer exists."

The judge set a jury trial for Nov. 3 on the charge of conspiring to commit murder and "international terrorism," starting in January 1994 and lasting until December 1995, when Sayegh allegedly traveled to a part of Saudi Arabia in an attempt to buy weapons and explosives.
U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan ordered that Sayegh, 28, a Shi'ite Muslim, remain in jail without bond.

After the court hearing, Carter told reporters he had attempted to negotiate a new plea deal with prosecutors but talks had broken off on Monday. He held out little hope that any agreement would be reached.

Carter maintained he had no information that Sayegh "knows about" the truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen and injured 500 at the Khobar Towers U.S. military housing complex on an airbase near Dhahran on Saudi Arabia's east coast.
Canadian court documents have identified Sayegh as the driver of a car that gave the truck a go-ahead signal to carry out the bombing.

Carter said he had no idea whether prosecutors would bring charges against Sayegh in the Khobar Towers bombing, but said the U.S. government had "no documentary evidence" linking Sayegh to the attack or any other criminal acts.

He said the indictment was based entirely on what Sayegh had told U.S. officials in Canada, but added that he would seek to have those statements thrown out on the grounds they were illegally obtained.
"The United States will have to look for documentary evidence from Saudi Arabia to support the indictment," he said.

If Sayegh is found innocent, Carter said he could be sent to a third country or he could seek political asylum in the United States. Sayegh's immigration lawyer has said he fears Sayegh would be executed if returned to Saudi Arabia.
